summary: Rochester Institute of Technology researchers used deep learning to study website-fingerprinting attacks against Tor, an anonymity network. They developed attack methods and evaluated countermeasures, including traffic obfuscation, to help improve users' privacy.
dilemmas: (i) Where did the training data come from, and did it include other people's browsing traffic?; (ii) Publishing a working attack that can identify Tor users vs. helping Tor build defenses; (iii) How much technical detail to release about a deanonymization method; (iv) Is it responsible to attack your own proposed defense, and who should see those results first?

summary: Three MIT students found vulnerabilities in the MBTA subway ticketing system as a class project and planned to present at DEF CON. The MBTA sued under the CFAA and obtained a gag order; it was later lifted.
dilemmas: (i) Research freedom vs. legal liability; (ii) Using litigation to suppress legitimate security findings; (iii) Free speech rights of security researchers; (iv) Responsible disclosure timeline

summary: Andrew Auernheimer and a collaborator automated requests to a publicly accessible AT&T interface and collected email addresses associated with approximately 114,000 iPad users. Auernheimer was convicted under U.S. computer-crime law, but an appeals court later overturned the conviction on venue grounds.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is scraping publicly accessible but unintended data unauthorized access under CFAA?; (ii) Responsible disclosure vs. media disclosure to maximize embarrassment; (iii) Chilling effect on legitimate security research; (iv) Corporate negligence vs. researcher culpability

summary: In 2006, Indiana University graduate student Christopher Soghoian created a publicly accessible fake airline boarding pass generator to expose vulnerabilities in airport security screening procedures. Although intended to demonstrate a security flaw and pressure authorities to address it, the tool could also enable individuals to bypass certain security checkpoints. The FBI subsequently raided his home, broke his front door glass, and seized his computers and other belongings. The investigation was eventually closed without criminal charges, raising ethical questions about public vulnerability disclosure, researcher responsibility, and the potential consequences of exposing security weaknesses.
outcome: FBI investigation closed; no criminal charges filed
dilemmas: (i) Is creating a working exploit to force policy change ethically justified?; (ii) Research freedom vs. real-world risk of tool misuse; (iii) Government pressure to suppress valid security findings; (iv) When does responsible disclosure become irresponsible provocation?

institution: Rick Wash Michigan & Molly Cooper / Michigan State University
summary: Rick Wash and Molly Cooper examined phishing-awareness training by sending simulated phishing emails to university employees without advance notice. Their research compared factual and story-based educational messages, raising questions about the use of deception, informed consent, and debriefing in cybersecurity experiments.
dilemmas: (i) Informed consent in deception-based cybersecurity experiments; (ii) Psychological harm to non-consenting participants; (iii) Whether IRBs are equipped to evaluate realistic cyber-deception studies; (iv) Institutional obligations when using own community as test subjects

summary: University of Minnesota researchers submitted intentionally flawed patches to Linux kernel maintainers without informing them that they were subjects of a security research experiment. The patches were rejected before being merged, but the experiment triggered a major controversy about research ethics and trust in open-source communities.
dilemmas: (i) Experimenting on open-source community without consent; (ii) Misuse of volunteer maintainer time; (iii) Risk of introducing real vulnerabilities into critical infrastructure; (iv) Publication of methods enabling similar attacks

summary: In 2014, the Tor Project identified a traffic-confirmation attack involving malicious Tor relays, while a related Carnegie Mellon University presentation about identifying Tor users was withdrawn from Black Hat. Allegations of law-enforcement involvement raised questions about research authorization, user consent, and disclosure; the precise relationship between the work and later investigations was contested.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Research on human subjects without consent; (ii) Withholding a vulnerability from the affected party (Tor Project); (iii) Financial incentives vs. ethical responsibility; (iv) Using academic research as outsourced law enforcement

summary: A Michigan security team authorized by DC election officials hacked a Washington DC internet voting pilot within 36 hours, gaining full control and modifying vote totals. DC cancelled the system; the team published full technical details.
dilemmas: (i) Does authorized pentesting of election infrastructure risk undermining public trust in democracy?; (ii) Full technical disclosure vs. limiting details that could enable copycat attacks; (iii) Academic freedom to publish results of authorized civic hacking; (iv) Coordination challenges between researchers, vendors, and election officials

institution: MedSec Holdings / Muddy Waters (St. Jude Medical)
summary: MedSec found serious vulnerabilities in St. Jude Medical cardiac implant devices. Rather than disclosing to the vendor, they partnered with investment firm Muddy Waters to short St. Jude's stock and released partial vulnerability details publicly.
dilemmas: (i) Financial conflict of interest in vulnerability disclosure; (ii) Potential patient risk from partial/premature disclosure; (iii) Bypassing coordinated disclosure entirely for profit; (iv) Whether short-selling on security research is legal/ethical

institution: David Levin / Vanguard Cybersecurity / Florida Elections
summary: Pen-tester David Levin tested SQL injection vulnerabilities on a Florida county elections website without written authorization and was arrested for unauthorized access.
dilemmas: (i) Unauthorized testing of public election infrastructure — crime or civic duty?; (ii) Whether pentesting without explicit written authorization can ever be 'ethical'; (iii) Chilling effect on election security research; (iv) Distinction between proof-of-concept testing and malicious intrusion

institution: Hacking Team Data Breach / Leak Ethics
summary: An unidentified hacker or hacking group compromised the Italian surveillance company Hacking Team and publicly released approximately 400 GB of internal data, including correspondence, customer information, source code, and exploits. The leak exposed the company's business relationships with governments accused of human rights abuses and created additional security risks by exposing attack tools.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Research ethics of using stolen/leaked corporate data; (ii) Whether exposing surveillance vendors justifies privacy violations of their employees; (iii) Researchers re-releasing zero-day exploits found in leaked data; (iv) Corporate accountability for selling offensive tools to authoritarian states

institution: J. Alex Halderman / Georgia Dominion Voting Machines
summary: University of Michigan researcher J. Alex Halderman examined Georgia's Dominion ImageCast X ballot-marking devices under court-authorized access and found vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to manipulate recorded votes under certain conditions. His findings raised concerns about election security, vulnerability remediation, and the potential misuse of security research to promote unfounded election fraud claims.
dilemmas: (i) Academic freedom vs. potential to fuel election misinformation; (ii) Whether sealed vulnerability research can remain secret in an adversarial legal setting; (iii) Risk that legitimate security findings are weaponized for political disinformation; (iv) Tension between public right to know and protecting public trust in elections

summary: Citizen Lab (University of Toronto) repeatedly identified and exposed governments using FinFisher spyware to surveil dissidents and journalists in Bahrain, Ethiopia, and Turkey, potentially tipping off targeted governments to improve their tradecraft.
dilemmas: (i) Does publishing detailed attribution of surveillance operations tip off abusive governments?; (ii) Researcher responsibility to notify both victims and software vendors; (iii) Balance between academic publication norms and protecting at-risk human rights defenders; (iv) Whether Western companies should face consequences for selling spyware to authoritarian buyers

institution: Justin Shafer / Patterson Dental / FBI Raids
summary: Texas dental IT researcher Shafer found patient health data on a publicly accessible anonymous FTP server and reported it responsibly. Patterson Dental complained to the FBI; Shafer's home was raided three times. He spent 8 months in pretrial detention on cyberstalking charges (for Facebook posts), ultimately pleading to one misdemeanor.
dilemmas: (i) 'Shoot the messenger' — vendor weaponizing CFAA against the person who exposed their negligence; (ii) Using cyberstalking statutes to silence researcher criticism of government overreach; (iii) Chilling effect: other researchers stopped disclosing after the raids; (iv) Pretrial detention as punishment before conviction

summary: Aaron Swartz downloaded millions of academic articles from JSTOR using MIT's network, reportedly intending to make research more widely accessible. Although JSTOR settled its civil dispute, federal prosecutors continued criminal charges under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and other statutes. Swartz died by suicide in January 2013 before trial.
outcome: Charged (case ended with death of defendant)
dilemmas: (i) CFAA overcriminalization — was exceeding ToS really a felony?; (ii) Prosecutorial overreach when the victim (JSTOR) dropped the case; (iii) Open-access ideology vs. intellectual property law; (iv) Criminal penalties disproportionate to actual harm

summary: Hutchins stopped the WannaCry ransomware by registering its kill-switch domain. Months later the FBI arrested him at DEF CON, alleging he helped develop the Kronos banking trojan in 2014–2015. He pleaded guilty to two CFAA counts and was sentenced to time served.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Should past black-hat activity negate subsequent white-hat contributions?; (ii) Arresting a researcher at a security conference as a deterrent tactic; (iii) Fairness of prosecuting juvenile/early-career offenses years later; (iv) Community trust in law enforcement collaboration with researchers

summary: QOMPLX relaunched PunkSpider at DEF CON — a tool that mass-crawls the web for SQL injection, XSS, and path-traversal vulnerabilities and publishes results in a searchable public database, exposing real flaws in Kickstarter and LendingTree before notification.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Public disclosure of vulnerabilities before vendor notification; (ii) Dual-use: security tool vs. attack enablement; (iii) Scanning sites without owner consent (potential CFAA exposure); (iv) Whether 'pressure through shame' is an ethical remediation strategy

institution: University of Michigan / FTP: The Forgotten Cloud
summary: University of Michigan researchers surveyed internet-facing FTP servers and found approximately 13.8 million servers, including 1.1 million allowing anonymous access. Their study documented exposures of sensitive files and the misuse of publicly writable FTP directories, raising questions about the ethics of internet-wide measurement.
dilemmas: (i) Ethical permissibility of internet-wide scanning without operator consent; (ii) Legal exposure under CFAA for automated access to systems not owned by researchers; (iii) Responsible disclosure when 1M+ vulnerable systems cannot all be notified; (iv) Dual-use: FBI used findings, but so did ransomware actors

institution: Ola Bini / Ecuador / Privacy Tool Developer
summary: Swedish programmer and privacy advocate Ola Bini was arrested in Ecuador in 2019 on computer-access allegations that he disputed. The proceedings, including an acquittal and later appeals, drew criticism from digital-rights groups. Ecuador revoked his visa and deported him to Sweden in October 2026, prompting renewed questions about due process and the treatment of security expertise.
dilemmas: (i) Criminalization of possession of security tools and technical literature as evidence of malicious intent; (ii) Politically motivated prosecution of security researchers; (iii) Due process rights of open-source developers; (iv) Chilling effect on privacy-tool development

institution: Logan Lamb / Kennesaw State University Election Server
summary: In 2016, security researcher Logan Lamb found that a misconfigured server operated by Kennesaw State University's Center for Election Systems exposed Georgia election files, including voter data and administrative credentials. The issue reportedly remained unresolved for months, and the server was later wiped amid election-security litigation; no altered election results were established.
outcome: No charges filed (KSU; evidence destruction concerns)
dilemmas: (i) Responsible disclosure failure when institutions do not respond to researcher notifications; (ii) Destruction of evidence after a researcher goes public; (iii) Whether researchers have an obligation to escalate beyond the institution when critical infrastructure is at risk; (iv) Accountability gap when election infrastructure is housed at an academic institution

institution: Jason Parker / Georgia Voter Cancellation Portal
summary: Independent researcher Jason Parker found a critical flaw in Georgia's online voter-cancellation portal: anyone knowing a voter's name, birth date, and county could cancel any voter's registration. He notified the Secretary of State's office; the office denied receiving the notification. ProPublica published the story; the flaw was quickly patched.
dilemmas: (i) When a government office denies receiving researcher notification, what recourse does the researcher have?; (ii) Timing of media disclosure for critical election infrastructure vulnerabilities; (iii) Risk that responsible disclosure of election bugs becomes fodder for disinformation; (iv) Whether election officials' denial of researcher contact constitutes bad faith

summary: During Operation Pacifier, the FBI took control of a Tor-hosted child sexual abuse material site and kept it operating for a limited period while deploying a court-authorized network investigative technique to identify visitors. The operation prompted challenges to the scope of the warrant, disclosure of investigative code, and the ethical costs of continuing to operate the site during the investigation.
outcome: Courts split on admissibility; some cases dropped
dilemmas: (i) Government use of malware as investigative technique without targeted warrants; (ii) Single warrant authorizing hacking of computers across 120+ countries; (iii) DOJ choosing to drop prosecutions rather than disclose offensive tools; (iv) Does fighting CSAM justify warrantless global hacking of Tor users?

summary: IOActive researchers found critical flaws in smart city infrastructure — traffic sensors, emergency-alert systems, water-control systems — through some unauthorized testing ('fire and forget' scan-and-test). Vendors were slow to patch; IOActive published technical details at DEF CON.
dilemmas: (i) Scanning municipal critical infrastructure without written permission; (ii) Full technical disclosure of infrastructure vulnerabilities when patches remain unavailable; (iii) Risk that published details of water/traffic attacks could cause physical harm; (iv) Whether researchers must wait longer when targets are critical infrastructure

summary: iSight Partners discovered Russian group Sandworm exploiting a Windows zero-day (CVE-2014-4114) to target NATO and Ukrainian government systems. iSight had used the intelligence for weeks before coordinating a patch release with Microsoft, monetizing it as a client intelligence product.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Private threat-intelligence firms monetizing zero-day knowledge vs. immediate public disclosure; (ii) Whether commercial security sector should have a legal disclosure obligation; (iii) Conflict between client confidentiality and warning undefended third parties; (iv) Government contractors holding offensive capabilities creates asymmetric vulnerability landscape

summary: University of Dhaka deployed an APNIC honeynet sensor exposing SSH and Telnet services and observed 63,247 attacks from 4,262 unique source IP addresses in 12 days, sharing threat-intelligence lessons.
dilemmas: (i) Ethical interaction with cybercriminals without encouraging illegal behavior; (ii) Entrapment vs. observation; (iii) Non-consent experimentation on criminals

summary: JHU researchers deployed high-interaction honeypots to study real attacker behavior and TTPs in depth.
dilemmas: (i) Ethical interaction with cybercriminals without encouraging illegal behavior; (ii) Entrapment vs. observation; (iii) Non-consent experimentation on criminals

summary: Former Tornado Development employee Bret McDanel warned of a webmail flaw that could expose customers' private messages. After the company failed to address it, he emailed thousands of customers directly; prosecutors treated the mass message as a computer offense. McDanel served a prison sentence before his conviction was overturned.
dilemmas: (i) Should warning customers about a security flaw ever count as a 'malicious code' offense?; (ii) What recourse exists for a wrongful felony conviction already served?; (iii) Chilling effect of CFAA's vague 'damage' language on good-faith disclosure

summary: After donating to a tsunami relief site and receiving no confirmation page, security consultant Daniel Cuthbert manually tested the donation page for phishing signs. He was convicted under the UK Computer Misuse Act and fined — the first such conviction under that section.
dilemmas: (i) Does intent matter under strict-liability computer-misuse statutes?; (ii) Should consumer self-protection checks ever be criminalized?; (iii) Career destruction disproportionate to harm caused

summary: Finisterre found DJI's wildcard SSL certificate and AWS keys exposed on GitHub, accessing customer flight logs, passports, and IDs. After reporting through DJI's bug bounty, DJI allegedly threatened CFAA charges and required a restrictive NDA before paying the $30,000 bounty. Finisterre declined and published the dispute publicly.
dilemmas: (i) Can bug bounty confidentiality terms be used to suppress legitimate findings?; (ii) Threatening prosecution against a researcher acting within a company's disclosed scope; (iii) Power imbalance between corporate legal teams and individual researchers

institution: Joseph Sullivan / Uber Data Breach Cover-Up
summary: Ten days after testifying to the FTC about Uber's security, Sullivan learned of a breach of 57M records. He arranged a $100K payment to hackers framed as a bug bounty and concealed the breach from the FTC. Convicted of obstruction and misprision of a felony; sentenced to three years' probation and $50K fine.
dilemmas: (i) Personal criminal liability of security executives for breach cover-ups; (ii) Where is the line between 'incident response' and witness tampering/concealment?; (iii) Should corporate leadership above the CSO share equal culpability?

institution: Flavio Garcia / University of Birmingham (VW & Thales)
summary: Garcia and Dutch colleagues cracked the Megamos Crypto algorithm used in vehicle immobilizers across 26 car brands. Volkswagen and Thales obtained a UK High Court injunction blocking publication for ~2 years; it was lifted after researchers agreed to redact a single sentence.
dilemmas: (i) Should a manufacturer be able to suppress academic publication of a flaw in its own product?; (ii) Reverse engineering legitimately purchased hardware vs. 'breach of confidence'; (iii) Public's right to know about car-theft vulnerabilities vs. risk of enabling theft

institution: Radboud University / Bart Jacobs (NXP / Mifare Classic)
summary: Radboud University researchers reverse-engineered NXP's MIFARE Classic chip, used in transit and building-access cards, and demonstrated weaknesses that could allow cards to be cloned. They alerted NXP and Dutch authorities before planned publication. NXP sought a court order to block disclosure, but a Dutch court ruled in favor of the researchers.
dilemmas: (i) Should commercial harm from a disclosed flaw ever justify suppressing peer-reviewed research?; (ii) Academic freedom vs. critical-infrastructure (transit) security concerns; (iii) Adequacy of advance confidential notification before publication

institution: Eric McCarty / University of Southern California
summary: McCarty exploited a SQL injection flaw in USC's online applicant database, downloading seven records from a database containing 275,000+ applicants' SSNs, before anonymously reporting it. He pleaded guilty to CFAA charges; sentenced to probation and $36,800 restitution.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Does proving a vulnerability by exploiting it cross from research into a prosecutable crime?; (ii) Proportionality of felony record/restitution vs. alerting the university; (iii) Effect of 'bragging' online on prosecutorial framing of intent

summary: Lynn resigned from ISS on the morning of his Black Hat talk to warn that Cisco routers could be exploited for a self-propagating 'router worm.' Cisco and ISS obtained a federal injunction barring further dissemination; Lynn agreed to a permanent injunction surrendering all related materials.
dilemmas: (i) Using copyright/trade-secret claims to suppress a security warning after the fact; (ii) Researcher's duty to disclose imminent internet-scale risk vs. employer's IP claims; (iii) Chilling effect of corporate legal muscle on conference speakers

summary: Teenage researcher Bill Demirkapi discovered significant vulnerabilities in school software potentially exposing millions of student and teacher records. When vendor outreach was ineffective, he sent a mass notification through a flawed school platform and received a two-day suspension.
dilemmas: (i) Is escalating to a mass alert ethical when normal disclosure channels are ignored by vendors?; (ii) Vendors using NDAs to control a minor researcher's ability to discuss findings; (iii) Industry-wide underinvestment in security for children's data

summary: Former Amazon Web Services employee Paige Thompson exploited a misconfiguration in Capital One's cloud environment in 2019 to obtain credentials and copy data affecting roughly 100 million people in the United States and six million in Canada. Prosecutors also alleged intrusions into other organizations and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining. She was convicted of wire fraud and computer-access offenses and was sentenced to time served, supervision, and restitution.
outcome: Convicted; time served, supervised release, and $40.745 million restitution
dilemmas: (i) Where is the line between legitimate cloud-misconfiguration research and felony data theft?; (ii) Should mental health and personal circumstances factor into sentencing for large-scale breaches?; (iii) Appellate oversight of 'too lenient' sentences for first-time offenders

summary: Volunteer research group Sakura Samurai targeted organizations with published VDPs, finding exposed credentials giving access to 100,000+ UN employee records and credentials across 26 Indian government departments. They limited actions to verification and disclosed through official channels; no charges were filed.
dilemmas: (i) Does scanning specifically because an org has a VDP make later 'out of scope' findings authorized?; (ii) Should past black-hat convictions disqualify someone from later legitimate research?; (iii) Reliance on government agencies to respond competently once notified

summary: Stefan Puffer detected an insecure wireless network associated with a Harris County court system and demonstrated access weaknesses to an official and reporter. Prosecutors alleged unauthorized access and damage, but a jury acquitted him.
dilemmas: (i) Should demonstrating a flaw to officials and media be treated identically to malicious intrusion?; (ii) Use of prosecution to deflect blame from the agency's own security failure; (iii) Jury nullification as a check on overbroad computer-crime statutes

institution: Clayton Taylor Dillard / Wake Internal Medicine (Wi-Fi)
summary: An IT consultant accessed an unsecured medical practice wireless network, obtained patient billing and insurance records, and contacted the press and patients directly to publicize the clinic's lax security. He pleaded guilty to wireless computer intrusion — the first such conviction in the US.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Why did near-identical facts (Puffer acquitted, Dillard convicted) produce opposite outcomes?; (ii) Contacting patients/press directly vs. notifying the practice first; (iii) Patient privacy harm from the disclosure method itself, separate from the underlying flaw

institution: Charlie Miller & Chris Valasek / Jeep Cherokee
summary: Researchers remotely disabled a Jeep's transmission and brakes over its cellular-connected infotainment system while a journalist drove on the highway. This forced a recall of ~1.4 million vehicles; owners filed a class-action suit against FCA alleging the company knew of the architectural flaw since 2011.
outcome: No charges filed; civil suit allowed to proceed
dilemmas: (i) Is a dramatic public stunt the only way to force a slow-moving manufacturer to patch a safety-critical flaw?; (ii) Consumer standing to sue over a vulnerability patched before real-world exploitation; (iii) Coupling safety-critical vehicle systems to internet-facing infotainment

institution: David Ross ('Connor Goodwolf') / City of Columbus Ransomware
summary: After ransomware actors exposed Columbus city data, cybersecurity researcher David Ross, known as Connor Goodwolf, publicly challenged official descriptions of the breach and warned that sensitive information was accessible. Columbus sued and obtained restrictions on disclosure, later dropping its lawsuit under conditions.
dilemmas: (i) Suing a whistleblower to manage a government's own breach-disclosure narrative; (ii) First Amendment limits on restraining someone from discussing already-public leaked data; (iii) Power asymmetry between a city government and an individual researcher

summary: After Newag-built passenger trains repeatedly stopped working following maintenance by independent repair shops, Polish research group Dragon Sector examined the train software and identified code associated with location and servicing-related lockouts. Newag denied wrongdoing and pursued legal claims against the researchers. The dispute highlights the tensions among software inspection, right to repair, and railway safety.
dilemmas: (i) Manufacturers using anti-repair 'DRM' embedded in safety-critical infrastructure; (ii) Suing researchers for exposing the lockout rather than addressing it (right-to-repair); (iii) Criminal investigations opened against disclosers rather than the manufacturer

institution: Wesley Wineberg / Facebook / Instagram Bug Bounty
summary: Bug hunter Wesley Wineberg reported critical Instagram infrastructure flaws after obtaining access to sensitive keys and files. Facebook disputed the extent of his testing, accusing him of exceeding bug-bounty boundaries; Wineberg alleged intimidating contact with his employer.
dilemmas: (i) Where does legitimate 'proof of impact' end and unauthorized data exfiltration begin within a bug bounty's scope?; (ii) Going around a researcher to pressure their employer instead of addressing the researcher directly; (iii) Ambiguity in bug bounty terms about how far a researcher may go to demonstrate severity

summary: A German IT professional discovered a shared database password embedded in Modern Solution software while investigating a customer problem, accessed an exposed database, and reported a vulnerability affecting data on roughly 700,000 consumers. Courts ruled that his access violated German criminal law.
dilemmas: (i) Should using a password the vendor itself left in plaintext constitute criminal 'unauthorized access'?; (ii) Criminalizing the verification step required to confirm a vulnerability is real; (iii) Disparity between vendor's negligence (unpunished) and researcher's penalty (criminal record)

summary: Perl programmer and Intel contractor Randal Schwartz copied password data and conducted unauthorized security testing that he said was intended to demonstrate weaknesses. He was convicted under Oregon computer crime law in the 1990s and later received an executive pardon.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Should 'improving security' justify unauthorized access against a former employer's systems?; (ii) Multi-decade reputational and financial cost of a later-overturned felony conviction; (iii) Employer's choice to pursue criminal prosecution rather than civil/internal remedies

summary: Russian ElcomSoft employee Sklyarov was arrested by the FBI immediately after his DEF CON talk on breaking Adobe eBook encryption — the first criminal charge under the DMCA. Held in custody then under travel restriction before a deal requiring his testimony against ElcomSoft in exchange for dropped charges.
outcome: Charged (charges dropped in exchange for testimony)
dilemmas: (i) Should conduct legal in a researcher's home country (Russia) trigger US criminal arrest at a US conference?; (ii) Conference attendance as a venue for law enforcement action against speakers; (iii) Using one defendant's testimony as leverage to convict their employer

institution: Matthew Green & bunnie Huang v. DOJ (DMCA / Section 1201)
summary: Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green and engineer Andrew 'bunnie' Huang filed a First Amendment challenge (via EFF) against Section 1201 of the DMCA, arguing it unconstitutionally prevented Green from publishing security research on commercial devices and Huang from building a legitimate video-stream device. Green said DMCA fear caused him to decline to investigate certain devices and chilled him from disclosing vulnerabilities. The DC Circuit ultimately upheld the DMCA's anti-circumvention provisions in 2024, finding they regulate conduct not speech.
dilemmas: (i) Does the DMCA's anti-circumvention provision unconstitutionally chill security research that requires bypassing DRM?; (ii) Should researchers be required to apply for triennial exemptions to do work that would otherwise be protected fair use?; (iii) How does the chilling effect of potential prosecution shape what security vulnerabilities get investigated and disclosed?; (iv) When researchers self-censor to avoid legal risk, who bears the cost in terms of undetected vulnerabilities?

institution: In Re Yahoo! Inc. Customer Data Security Breach Litigation
summary: Lawsuits followed major Yahoo account breaches from 2013 onward and allegations of insufficient cybersecurity and delayed notification. Consumers challenged whether the company adequately protected and informed its users.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) At what point does delayed breach disclosure cross from incident response into material omission for securities fraud?; (ii) What is a CSO/CISO's personal duty when corporate leadership decides to delay disclosure?; (iii) Acquisition context: does a pending merger change the calculus of when a breach must be disclosed?; (iv) Are current securities laws adequate to deter corporate concealment of large-scale breaches?

institution: In Re Okta, Inc. Securities Litigation
summary: After screenshots posted by Lapsus$ in March 2022 revealed an earlier compromise involving an Okta customer-support contractor, Okta faced criticism over the timing and clarity of its public disclosures. Investors filed securities litigation alleging misleading statements about security and the incident. A separate 2023 breach of Okta's support system should not be conflated with this case.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) When a company minimizes a breach publicly while knowing the full scope internally, is that fraud or legitimate incident response?; (ii) What is the appropriate disclosure timeline when breach scope is still being investigated?; (iii) Does downplaying a breach to avoid stock impact constitute securities fraud even if the company later corrects the record?; (iv) How should security executives balance legal counsel's advice against ethical obligations to customers?

summary: Following Equifax's 2017 data breach, investors brought a securities class action alleging misleading public statements about the company's security practices and risk exposure. The case was resolved through a civil settlement; it did not result in a criminal conviction in this litigation.
dilemmas: (i) Does selling stock after learning of a breach but before public disclosure constitute insider trading, regardless of intent?; (ii) What personal criminal liability do security executives bear for their company's breach concealment?; (iii) Should a CISO who discovers a breach be required to immediately notify the board even if doing so triggers premature disclosure?; (iv) Are mandatory breach disclosure timelines the right policy lever, or do they just create liability without improving security?

summary: The 2014–2015 Office of Personnel Management breaches exposed sensitive information about more than 21 million people, including federal employees and applicants for security clearances. The American Federation of Government Employees and others brought suit over the government's protection of this data; a federal appeals court reinstated some claims after an initial dismissal.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Civil litigation; some claims reinstated on appeal
dilemmas: (i) What duty of care does a government agency owe its employees when it holds their most sensitive personal and national security data?; (ii) When repeated security warnings are ignored and a catastrophic breach occurs, who bears personal accountability?; (iii) Should federal employees whose security clearance files were stolen have a right to sue for damages?; (iv) Does sovereign immunity effectively shield government agencies from accountability for catastrophic security failures?

summary: hiQ, a data analytics company, scraped public LinkedIn profiles using automated bots to build workforce analytics products. LinkedIn sent a cease-and-desist and blocked hiQ's access. hiQ sued; the Ninth Circuit twice ruled that scraping publicly accessible data likely does not violate the CFAA because 'without authorization' requires a gate/barrier the scraper bypassed. The Supreme Court vacated and remanded in light of Van Buren. Ultimately hiQ settled, agreeing to a $500K judgment and permanent injunction after LinkedIn won on breach-of-contract grounds using fake profile creation.
dilemmas: (i) Is scraping publicly accessible data 'unauthorized access' under the CFAA if no password or authentication barrier was bypassed?; (ii) Can a company weaponize the CFAA to prevent a competitor from accessing data that users themselves made public?; (iii) Where is the line between lawful data collection for research/analysis and commercial exploitation of user-generated public data?; (iv) Does the CFAA's broad interpretation give large platforms de facto monopoly control over public data?

institution: Universal City Studios v. Corley / Reimerdes (DeCSS / DMCA)
summary: 2600 Magazine publisher Eric Corley (Emmanuel Goldstein) posted the DeCSS code — a program that decrypted DVD copy protection — on his website and linked to other sites hosting it. The movie studios sued under the DMCA's anti-trafficking provision. The Second Circuit upheld the injunction, ruling that computer code posting is regulable conduct under intermediate First Amendment scrutiny and that the DMCA's anti-trafficking provision was constitutional. The case became the defining early test of whether publishing security-relevant code is protected speech.
dilemmas: (i) Is publishing functional security/encryption code protected First Amendment speech?; (ii) Can the DMCA's anti-trafficking provision constitutionally prohibit publication of code that has legitimate research and interoperability uses?; (iii) Does linking to a site hosting prohibited code make a publisher liable under the DMCA?; (iv) Who gets to define the boundary between security research tools and circumvention devices?

institution: DVD Copy Control Assn v. Bunner (DeCSS — California)
summary: Andrew Bunner posted DeCSS code that could circumvent DVD copy protection. The DVD Copy Control Association sought an injunction under California trade-secret law. The California Supreme Court held that an injunction could be compatible with free-speech protections if the information remained a protected trade secret; on remand, the injunction was ultimately set aside.
dilemmas: (i) Can trade secret law justify a prior restraint on publication of security-relevant code that has already spread widely on the internet?; (ii) At what point does information become 'too public' to still qualify as a protectable trade secret?; (iii) Does the First Amendment protect redistribution of security code even if the original acquisition was improper?; (iv) Should courts balance the chilling effect on security research before granting injunctions against code publication?

institution: Davidson & Associates v. Jung (Battle.net / bnetd reverse engineering)
summary: Developers reverse-engineered Blizzard's Battle.net gaming service to build 'bnetd,' a free open-source server that let players run their own game servers. Blizzard sued under the DMCA and breach of the end-user license agreement (EULA). The Eighth Circuit ruled against the developers, finding that the EULA's prohibition on reverse engineering was enforceable and that reverse engineering to achieve interoperability did not qualify for the DMCA's interoperability exception because the developers had agreed to the EULA. The case chilled open-source interoperability work.
dilemmas: (i) Can an EULA contractually waive the DMCA's statutory right to reverse engineer for interoperability?; (ii) Is building a compatible open-source alternative to a proprietary service a legitimate security/research activity or IP infringement?; (iii) Should agreeing to a ToS/EULA strip a researcher of rights they would otherwise have under the DMCA's interoperability exception?; (iv) How does this ruling affect security researchers who need to reverse-engineer software they've licensed to find vulnerabilities?

institution: Bernstein v. US Dept. of State
summary: Daniel Bernstein challenged U.S. export regulations that required government approval before he could publish his encryption algorithm, Snuffle, and its source code. Bernstein argued that these restrictions violated his First Amendment rights by treating academic research and computer code as regulated exports. In 1999, a Ninth Circuit panel ruled in his favor, recognizing encryption source code as protected speech. However, the opinion was subsequently withdrawn for rehearing, and the case was remanded following changes to export regulations, leaving the broader constitutional questions unresolved.
outcome: Civil challenge; panel opinion withdrawn and case remanded
dilemmas: (i) Is encryption source code 'speech' protected by the First Amendment, or purely functional 'conduct' that can be regulated without First Amendment scrutiny?; (ii) Can the government require a license before a researcher publishes an academic paper containing functional encryption code?; (iii) Do national security interests in controlling encryption export justify prior restraint on academic publication?; (iv) How should the law treat dual-use academic research that has both civilian security value and potential military/intelligence applications?

summary: During litigation over mismanagement of Native American trust accounts, a court-appointed investigation identified serious weaknesses in Department of the Interior computer security. In 2001, a federal judge ordered systems holding or able to access individual Indian trust data to disconnect from the internet until their security could be assessed.
dilemmas: (i) Can a court order a government agency to disconnect from the internet as a security remedy?; (ii) What accountability mechanisms exist when a government agency's repeated security failures endanger the financial data of a vulnerable population?; (iii) Who should conduct security audits of government systems — internal auditors, independent experts, or adversarial testers?; (iv) When a security audit reveals catastrophic failure, how should findings be disclosed without creating additional risk?

institution: Verkada Camera Breach / Tillie Kottmann / FTC
summary: In 2021, hackers accessed Verkada's cloud-camera infrastructure, exposing live feeds and other sensitive information from customer sites. The incident was attributed to hacker Tillie Kottmann, who faced separate federal charges relating to hacking activity. In 2024, the FTC required security improvements and a $2.95 million civil penalty for unrelated commercial-email violations; that dollar amount was not a fine for the camera breach.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Federal hacking indictment; FTC security order and separate CAN-SPAM penalty
dilemmas: (i) Is breaching a surveillance company to expose its reach a form of protected political/security activism or straightforward criminal hacking?; (ii) Does the target being a surveillance company change the ethical calculus of an unauthorized breach?; (iii) What accountability should cloud security camera vendors face when their poor security exposes sensitive environments like hospitals and prisons?; (iv) When a vendor's negligence enables mass surveillance exposure, who bears moral responsibility — the hacker or the vendor?

institution: Microsoft / Nightmare Eclipse (Windows Defender & BitLocker Zero-Days)
summary: In 2026, a researcher using the name Nightmare Eclipse released proof-of-concept code for multiple Windows vulnerabilities after alleging problems with Microsoft's disclosure and bounty process. Some techniques were later observed in intrusions, and Microsoft criticized the uncoordinated publication of exploitable flaws. Claims of account deletion, retaliation, and threatened prosecution should be attributed to the parties rather than treated as independently established facts.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) When a company allegedly mistreats a researcher — deleting their account, withholding bounty payments, removing attribution — does that researcher bear ethical responsibility for subsequently publishing unpatched vulnerabilities?; (ii) Is 'full disclosure' of an unpatched vulnerability ever ethically justified as a last resort against an unresponsive or hostile vendor?; (iii) Does threatening a researcher with criminal prosecution for disclosing bugs create a chilling effect that ultimately harms users more than the disclosure itself?; (iv) Who bears moral responsibility when a researcher-disclosed vulnerability is exploited in the wild — the researcher or the vendor that failed to patch it?

summary: Academic researchers published a holistic study of WinPot ATM jackpotting malware — a strain used by criminal groups to force ATMs to dispense cash — analyzing its attack vectors, exploitation techniques, and defensive countermeasures in detail. The paper provided comprehensive technical documentation of how ATM jackpotting works, raising dual-use concerns that the level of technical detail could serve as an implementation guide for criminal actors even as it aimed to advance defensive knowledge.
dilemmas: (i) How much technical detail is appropriate in academic publications about criminal malware when the same detail that helps defenders also helps attackers?; (ii) Should researchers publishing analyses of criminal tools be required to coordinate with affected vendors (ATM manufacturers, banks) before publication?; (iii) Is studying and publishing criminal malware ethically different from studying and publishing proof-of-concept researcher-written exploits?; (iv) What responsibility do academic publishers and program committees bear for the dual-use risk of papers they accept?

summary: AI ethics researcher Timnit Gebru disputed Google management over a research paper criticizing the risks and limitations of large language models. Her December 2020 departure sparked a public debate about corporate influence on critical research.
dilemmas: (i) Corporate influence over AI ethics research; (ii) Academic freedom vs. employer interests; (iii) Suppression of critical AI research; (iv) Research independence

institution: Nasr, Carlini et al. / ChatGPT Training Data Extraction
summary: Researchers demonstrated that ChatGPT could reveal portions of its training data through carefully crafted prompts.
dilemmas: (i) Publishing techniques that could be abused; (ii) AI transparency vs. misuse; (iii) Responsible disclosure for foundation models

summary: Former OpenAI engineer Suchir Balaji publicly challenged the legality and ethics of training commercial generative AI systems on copyrighted works, arguing that resulting tools may compete with creators whose works they use.
dilemmas: (i) Whistleblowing vs. confidentiality; (ii) Copyright in AI training; (iii) Corporate accountability

summary: Robert Williams was wrongfully arrested after being misidentified by facial recognition software.
dilemmas: (i) Reliability of facial recognition; (ii) Civil rights; (iii) Government accountability; (iv) AI bias

summary: ACLU sued Clearview AI over scraping billions of facial images without consent.
dilemmas: (i) Mass biometric surveillance; (ii) Privacy; (iii) Consent; (iv) Commercial surveillance

summary: Apple sued Corellium over virtualized iOS technology used by security researchers to inspect software and test vulnerabilities. Courts considered copyright and fair-use issues, and an appeals court held that Corellium's virtualization could qualify as fair use while remanding some issues. The dispute illustrates how intellectual-property enforcement can affect security research tools.
outcome: Civil copyright litigation; substantial fair-use ruling for Corellium
dilemmas: (i) Copyright vs. security research; (ii) Research tool legality; (iii) Vendor retaliation

summary: Researchers were threatened with DMCA litigation for publishing research on breaking digital watermarking.
dilemmas: (i) DMCA chilling research; (ii) Academic freedom; (iii) Disclosure rights

summary: Student and critic Erik Johnson published material criticizing Proctorio’s remote exam-monitoring software. Proctorio used copyright claims against excerpts used in criticism; the ensuing legal dispute raised concerns about fair use, surveillance, and attempts to silence scrutiny.
dilemmas: (i) Abuse of copyright law; (ii) Research criticism; (iii) Chilling effects

institution: Dennis Giese and Braelynn Luedtke / Digilock
summary: Before DEF CON 2024, security researchers Dennis Giese and Braelynn Luedtke received a cease-and-desist demand from electronic-lock maker Digilock over their planned presentation on vulnerabilities in keyless locks. The talk was postponed briefly while lawyers reviewed the dispute, then proceeded. This was a lock-security disclosure dispute, not a robot-vacuum dispute.
dilemmas: (i) Corporate retaliation; (ii) Responsible disclosure; (iii) Research freedom

summary: Researcher downloaded publicly exposed government records and was criminally charged.
dilemmas: (i) Publicly accessible data; (ii) Criminalizing research; (iii) Government accountability

summary: Colombian graduate student was prosecuted for sharing an academic paper online.
dilemmas: (i) Open access; (ii) Copyright; (iii) Academic freedom

summary: Journalist discovered exposed teacher SSNs in webpage source code and was publicly accused of hacking.
dilemmas: (i) Viewing source code vs. hacking; (ii) Government retaliation; (iii) Press freedom

institution: Andrew Lemon / Traffic Signal Controller Disclosure
summary: Security researcher Andrew Lemon reported that he found a critical vulnerability in a traffic-signal controller he had purchased secondhand. According to his public account, the vendor's lawyers responded with threats of prosecution and disputed his authorization to test the equipment, rather than engaging directly with the reported issue.
dilemmas: (i) Legal intimidation; (ii) Responsible disclosure; (iii) Chilling effect

summary: Following reporting on a critical vulnerability in a Keeper password-manager browser extension, Keeper Security sued Ars Technica and reporter Dan Goodin, disputing aspects of the coverage. The suit raised concerns about vendors using litigation in response to security journalism.
dilemmas: (i) SLAPP lawsuits; (ii) Vendor accountability; (iii) Journalism and disclosure

institution: FreeHour / Malta Students (Grigolo, Debono, Scerri, Collins)
summary: Four computer-science students reported vulnerabilities in the FreeHour student timetabling app with a 90-day disclosure window and asked whether the report might qualify for a bounty once fixed. FreeHour went to police; three students had their homes searched, were strip-searched and had devices seized. The company said the mention of payment, changes to the app's front end and the 90-day 'ultimatum' led its lawyers to treat the report as a threat.
dilemmas: (i) Stating a disclosure deadline is standard practice, but paired with a payment question it can read as coercion: how should researchers state a timeline and ask about bounties without appearing to extort? (ii) Was altering the app's front end necessary to prove the flaw, or did it go beyond what proof required? (iii) Should a company with no disclosure policy be expected to recognize good-faith research, or is caution toward unsolicited reports reasonable?

institution: Coalfire / Iowa Judicial Branch & Dallas County Sheriff
summary: The Iowa state court administration hired Coalfire to test the physical security of its courthouses. During an authorized after-hours test, the Dallas County sheriff arrested employees Gary DeMercurio and Justin Wynn and charged them with burglary, disputing the state's authority over a county building. Charges were dropped on January 30, 2020, four months later.
dilemmas: (i) Whose permission counts when the client authorizes a test but another authority controls the premises? (ii) When scope is ambiguous mid-engagement, should testers stop or proceed on the client's written word? (iii) Does publicizing the arrest protect future testers, or make clients less willing to authorize physical testing?

summary: Tokarev submitted four iOS vulnerabilities to Apple's bug bounty between March and May 2021. After one was patched silently and he received neither credit nor payment, he published three unpatched zero-days with proof-of-concept code. Apple later sent DMCA takedowns over a documentation site he had mirrored, and credited one bug (CVE-2021-30871) in October 2021.
dilemmas: (i) Does a vendor breaking its bounty promises justify releasing unpatched zero-days that expose millions of users? (ii) Were the later DMCA takedowns legitimate IP enforcement or retaliation for the disclosure? (iii) Should bounty programs be held to enforceable timelines for credit and payment?

summary: Arm filed abuse reports and cease-and-desist demands over Markstedter's long-running educational domains, such as arm-assembly.com, which taught Arm assembly and exploitation. Her registrar took the domains down; she transferred the 'arm' domains to Arm and rebranded, despite years of known use and past talks given inside the company.
dilemmas: (i) Trademark enforcement versus the public value of independent security education about a vendor's platform. (ii) Should researchers build educational resources on a vendor's brand name they don't control? (iii) Does a long, friendly working relationship change what either side owes the other?

summary: Rapid7, acting on Ford's behalf in a brand-protection effort, emailed NahamSec claiming one of his YouTube videos was illegal and that he was aiding criminals, and asked him to remove it. He replied that he had done nothing wrong and declined to remove it immediately.
dilemmas: (i) Where does educational hacking content end and enabling fraud begin? (ii) Should brand-protection services treat security education as a threat by default? (iii) Should a security company take takedown work aimed at other researchers?

summary: During Germany's 2021 federal election campaign, Wittmann found and published data-security problems in the campaign app used by the CDU, CSU and Austria's ÖVP. The CDU filed a criminal complaint against her, then withdrew it and apologized after public outcry.
dilemmas: (i) Publishing flaws in a party's app during an election: public interest in voter-data security versus influence on the campaign. (ii) Should political parties be held to the same disclosure expectations as vendors? (iii) Does Germany's anti-hacking law leave good-faith researchers too exposed to complaints like this?

summary: what3words, which sells its location-addressing system to emergency services, threatened the WhatFreeWords open-source reimplementation in 2019. In April 2021 Toponce received a legal letter demanding he stop sharing the software after researchers had analyzed how the wordlist could produce confusable addresses.
dilemmas: (i) Proprietary algorithms used by emergency services versus the public's interest in independent analysis of how they fail. (ii) Is sharing a reimplementation of a company's method legitimate research or IP infringement? (iii) How should researchers weigh legal risk when the safety stakes are public?

summary: Dyke found sensitive information in a public GitHub repository of the Apperta Foundation, an NHS-backed nonprofit, and reported it. Apperta reported him to Northumbria Police and revoked licenses on materials he used.
dilemmas: (i) How much should a researcher look at exposed data to confirm a leak before reporting it? (ii) Reporting the finder to police: reasonable caution or blame-shifting by the organization that leaked? (iii) Do publicly funded health projects owe more transparency about their own mistakes?

summary: Rigo's Infiltrate 2021 talk on vulnerabilities in Xerox multifunction printers was cancelled an hour before it was due, citing pending legal action. He gave the talk on April 22, 2021.
dilemmas: (i) Should vendors be able to use last-minute legal threats to delay talks on already-reported flaws? (ii) What do conferences owe speakers facing legal pressure? (iii) When a vendor objects, does delaying a talk serve users or only the vendor?

summary: Saskia Coplans of Digital Interruption tried to report a vulnerability in the women-only Giggle app that exposed users' account information, including location data and photos, first through Twitter direct messages. Giggle's CEO denied the issue for days, blocked the researchers and threatened legal action, then issued a conciliatory statement; the bug was eventually patched without acknowledgment.
dilemmas: (i) Is reaching out over Twitter an acceptable disclosure channel when a vendor has no security contact? (ii) When a vendor denies a flaw exposing vulnerable users, how quickly should researchers go public? (iii) How should researchers respond when a disclosure becomes entangled in a political dispute about the app?

summary: Jackson found that promo codes belonging to companies that had paid for Talkspace's therapy service let anyone sign up for free. Talkspace denied the claim and sent him a cease-and-desist letter.
dilemmas: (i) Is a business-logic flaw like promo-code abuse a security vulnerability worth disclosing, or a billing issue? (ii) Proving the flaw meant using another company's paid codes: necessary proof or misuse? (iii) Should a mental-health platform's denial and legal threat be weighed against its users' trust?

summary: Kubecka reported finding serious weaknesses in Boeing's network, including internet-exposed test environments, malware infections and XSS flaws, and spoke publicly about them. Boeing, which had no disclosure policy, allegedly threatened legal action to stop her speaking and considered damaging her reputation.
dilemmas: (i) When a company with no disclosure policy ignores safety-relevant findings, is a public talk justified? (ii) How much detail about an aviation manufacturer's network weaknesses is safe to share publicly? (iii) Does a researcher's status (veteran, well-known speaker) change how the vendor should respond?

summary: At 16, Demirkapi found a 4 GB WordPress debug log exposed on a public MIT service and reported it. An MIT staff member warned him of up to five years in jail and said he had caused significant disruption; MIT's IT head called his scanning 'problematic.'
dilemmas: (i) Is scanning a university's public services to find exposures acceptable without permission? (ii) How should institutions respond when the reporter is a minor? (iii) Threatening jail for a good-faith report: does it protect the institution or discourage the next student?

summary: An 18-year-old reported flaws in Budapest's new e-ticket system, including plain-text password emails, an IDOR exposing other users' data, ticket cloning, price manipulation and an admin password of 'adminadmin.' He was arrested; BKK claimed his report went to the wrong address, which he disputed with a screenshot. The arrest drew thousands of one-star reviews and a 500-person protest.
dilemmas: (i) How can a researcher prove a price-manipulation flaw without committing fare fraud? (ii) When a vendor disputes receiving a report, who bears the burden of proof? (iii) Does public outrage protect researchers, or harden institutions against them?

summary: In 2016, before Chase had a disclosure program, Scira found that transferring Ultimate Rewards points under unstable network conditions could create unlimited points. He ran experiments while reporting them to Chase's support account on Twitter, and the issues were fixed. About a week later Chase sent a hostile email and closed his accounts, including checking and savings, and accounts of family members. He disclosed the story in 2020.
dilemmas: (i) Converting test points to cash while reporting: proof of impact or fraud? (ii) With no disclosure program, is reporting through a customer-support Twitter account an adequate channel? (iii) Is closing family members' accounts risk management or retaliation?

institution: ESNC GmbH / PwC (ACE software for SAP)
summary: ESNC tried to coordinate disclosure of vulnerabilities in PwC's ACE software for SAP that could enable accounting fraud. PwC sent two cease-and-desist letters; ESNC published the vulnerabilities with a timeline anyway.
dilemmas: (i) Should researchers publish after a cease-and-desist when the flaw could enable financial fraud? (ii) Does an auditing firm's own software deserve stricter scrutiny? (iii) How much detail is safe when the affected systems run companies' financial controls?

summary: Jensen found an enumeration flaw in Nerium's customer portal that let any customer see others' details, including payment and address information. Nerium ignored his reports and contacted him only after he posted enough detail to prove the issue, with a cease-and-desist letter. He replaced the post with a timeline.
dilemmas: (i) How much detail must be public to force a non-responsive company to act, and how much is too much? (ii) Should researchers comply with a takedown demand when users remain exposed? (iii) Does exposing payment data change the duty to warn affected customers?

summary: Høyer found vulnerabilities in the system his son's kindergarten used. He was accused of accessing other children's sensitive information, which he denied, and was charged rather than the flaws being fixed. He was convicted in local court and acquitted on appeal in March 2017 for lack of evidence.
dilemmas: (i) A parent checking a system holding their child's data: protective duty or unauthorized access? (ii) How far can a researcher verify a flaw involving children's records? (iii) Should prosecutors pursue the reporter when the vendor's security is the real failure?

summary: Gnesa withdrew his Hack in the Box GSEC talk on surveillance camera vulnerabilities after a legal threat from one of the three vendors involved, despite having privately disclosed the flaws to the vendor in advance.
dilemmas: (i) If a vendor was warned privately, does it still have standing to block a talk? (ii) Should researchers withdraw talks under threat, or present and risk a lawsuit? (iii) Who protects the camera owners while the research stays unpublished?

summary: modzero reported flaws in Good for Enterprise, including an XSS in the admin console and later a remotely exploitable account-hijacking bug in its mobile device management suite. Good threatened legal action against publication, citing its license terms barring reverse engineering.
dilemmas: (i) Can a license agreement legitimately bar the security research that protects the product's customers? (ii) Should researchers publish against a vendor's license-based objection? (iii) When enterprise security software is itself vulnerable, who should decide disclosure timing?

summary: slipstream published details and a working exploit for a vulnerability in Impero Education Pro, classroom-monitoring software installed on school computers. Impero's lawyers alleged breach of the user agreement, disclosure of confidential information and reputational damage. The information stayed public.
dilemmas: (i) Full disclosure of a working exploit for software on children's school computers: pressure on the vendor or risk to students? (ii) Should researchers coordinate first even with vendors they expect to be hostile? (iii) Is a user agreement a valid basis for silencing security findings?

summary: Sorianello saw a publicly posted SSL certificate flaw in the Vot.ar electronic voting system and reported it to vendor MSA as a warning; he had not found or published it. After a different group published another Vot.ar vulnerability, police raided his home on a judge's order.
dilemmas: (i) Does reporting someone else's public finding expose the reporter to liability? (ii) During an election, should authorities treat reporters of flaws as suspects or allies? (iii) How should researchers protect themselves when warning a vendor about issues they didn't discover?

summary: A law firm representing CyberLock threatened a DMCA-based lawsuit over Davis's research into cloning CyberKey high-security keys. A day after the threat became public, IOActive published the advisory.
dilemmas: (i) Should anti-circumvention law cover research into physical security products? (ii) Publishing the day after a public threat: principled stand or escalation? (iii) What do owners of high-security locks need to know, and when?

summary: Rigo cancelled his SyScan 2015 talk on Blue Coat ProxySG after pressure from Blue Coat, passed on through the conference founder. He later presented the research at Ruxcon and Black Hat Europe.
dilemmas: (i) When pressure comes through a conference organizer rather than a lawyer, is it still a threat? (ii) Should an employer's relationship with a vendor decide when its researcher speaks? (iii) Did the delay protect anyone, or only postpone the inevitable?

summary: After Bourbon sent details of vulnerabilities in FireEye's Malware Analysis System to Exploit-DB, he was suspended from his day job, reportedly under pressure from FireEye, which denied involvement. FireEye later patched the issues and credited him.
dilemmas: (i) Is sending findings straight to a public exploit database fair to the vendor's customers? (ii) Should a vendor ever contact a researcher's employer over independent work? (iii) Should employers shield staff from vendor pressure over research done on their own time?

institution: Kristian Hermansen & Matt Ploessel / Covered California
summary: The researchers found security flaws in Covered California, the state's health-insurance exchange website. Their video about the flaws was taken down from YouTube, and the FBI visited them and asked them to stop discussing the issues.
dilemmas: (i) Public video first versus private report first for a government health site holding sensitive data. (ii) Is an FBI request to stop talking a legitimate safety measure or intimidation? (iii) How should researchers balance public trust in a new public program against users' right to know?

summary: Rogers, a schoolboy, found security flaws in the Public Transport Victoria website that exposed customer data and reported them. PTV referred the incident to Victoria Police.
dilemmas: (i) Should a teenager's good-faith report be handled differently from an adult's? (ii) Police referral as a default response: protecting customers or deterring reporters? (iii) How much access is acceptable to confirm customer data is exposed?

summary: Wood published an insecure data storage issue in ZippyYum's iOS Subway ordering app on the Full Disclosure mailing list. Anticipating legal action, he noted he had signed no NDA and retained an attorney.
dilemmas: (i) Full disclosure on a public list versus private notice for a consumer payment app. (ii) Should researchers retain counsel before publishing? (iii) Do customers' interests favor speed or coordination when card data may be stored insecurely?

summary: Turner reported flaws in Christchurch's Metrocard bus fare system to Environment Canterbury; three months later nothing had been fixed, and he disclosed them at Kiwicon 7. ECan called the police, and claims followed that about 70,000 free rides had been taken.
dilemmas: (i) After three months of inaction, was a public talk the right lever? (ii) If disclosure led to widespread fare evasion, who bears responsibility: the researcher or the operator who didn't fix it? (iii) How much technical detail is appropriate for a transit-fare flaw?

summary: Secunia reported a use-after-free bug in VLC Media Player. VideoLAN threatened legal action and disputed whether it was patched; Secunia changed its advisory to 'patched' and then back to 'unpatched' after further analysis, and both sides published accounts of the dispute.
dilemmas: (i) When vendor and researcher disagree on whether a bug is fixed, whose claim should users trust? (ii) Can an open-source project threaten legal action without undermining its own community norms? (iii) Should an advisory ever change status under legal pressure?

summary: After two weeks without a patch, a researcher told Zamfoo he would post a proof of concept if the fix didn't come faster. Zamfoo threatened to sue him.
dilemmas: (i) A two-week deadline with a public proof of concept: fair pressure or an ultimatum? (ii) How short can a disclosure deadline be before it becomes coercion? (iii) Does threatening a PoC change how a vendor will read the researcher's intent?

summary: Fox-IT reported unencrypted storage of confidential data in Keeper's iOS password manager within 24 hours of finding it. Keeper refused to engage, sent all communication to its lawyers, and warned that public disclosure could meet swift legal action. Fox-IT published an advisory.
dilemmas: (i) When a vendor responds only through lawyers, does the researcher still owe it coordination? (ii) Should a vendor's claim that an update fixed the issue be accepted without detail? (iii) Is publishing against a legal warning justified for a password manager whose users can't assess the risk?

summary: Al-Khabaz, a student, found a flaw in the Omnivox portal that exposed about 250,000 students' records and reported it to his college. Skytech threatened to press charges and send him to jail unless he signed an NDA, and he was later expelled.
dilemmas: (i) Is re-testing a reported system to check the fix diligence or new unauthorized access? (ii) Is demanding an NDA under threat of prosecution ever acceptable? (iii) Should a school discipline a student for reporting a flaw in software it bought?

summary: Langner's talk on nuclear power plant SCADA vulnerabilities was cancelled at the last minute at the 12th ICS Cyber Security Conference after a vendor objected and threatened to sue, even though plant officials had approved the presentation.
dilemmas: (i) If the plant operator approves disclosure, should the equipment vendor still have a veto? (ii) How much detail about nuclear-plant control systems is safe for a public audience? (iii) Does silencing ICS research make plants safer or just less informed?

summary: E-Soft sent YouTube a copyright claim to remove Romang's video demonstrating a Metasploit exploit module for its Digital Music Pad software. The video was reposted and remained available.
dilemmas: (i) Is a copyright claim against an exploit demo a legitimate use of IP law? (ii) Are video demonstrations of working exploits a responsible way to publicize flaws? (iii) Should platforms review takedowns aimed at security research?

summary: Weber cancelled the ShmooCon 2012 release of a free smart-meter security testing tool, citing a wish to work with the vendor, and later presented at BSidesLV 2012. A source told Attrition that InGuardians contacted the vendor only weeks after the CFP, raising the possibility the vendor became a client.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) When a vendor becomes a client, can the researcher still decide disclosure independently? (ii) Should a testing tool for critical infrastructure be released freely? (iii) Is it fair to the community to withdraw a scheduled talk for commercial reasons?

summary: Eckhart documented that Carrier IQ software installed on phones logged excessive user information. Carrier IQ sent him a cease-and-desist letter, then retracted it after EFF involvement and negative attention. The research stayed public.
dilemmas: (i) Public interest in exposing hidden phone tracking versus a vendor's claim of confidentiality. (ii) Should privacy findings about software users can't remove go straight to the public? (iii) What changed the outcome: the law, or public pressure?

summary: Webster found a direct object reference flaw in his pension fund's website exposing other members' information and reported it. First State Super reported him to police and threatened further legal action, then withdrew the threat after negative publicity.
dilemmas: (i) How many other members' records is it acceptable to view to show a flaw is real? (ii) Should a fund be able to make the reporter pay for its own security failures? (iii) Does public pressure, rather than law, end up deciding these cases?

institution: Brenno de Winter / Trans Link Systems (OV-chipkaart)
summary: Journalist Brenno de Winter demonstrated weaknesses in the Dutch OV-chipkaart transit payment systemby manipulating card balances and traveling with modified cards. He was questioned by police after a complaint by the system's operator, Trans Link Systems. However, the prosecutors subsequently decided not to pursue criminal charges. The dispute raised questions about reporting security flaws in public services.
dilemmas: (i) Should journalists demonstrate a transit-card flaw themselves to prove a story? (ii) Is prosecuting a reporter a proportionate response to fare fraud risk? (iii) Where is the line between investigative journalism and exploitation?

summary: Researchers reported a buffer overflow in Magix Music Maker 16 and were threatened under Germany's anti-hacking law. They published anyway and persuaded Magix to change its stance; Magix opened a researcher portal whose terms bar disclosure before a fix.
dilemmas: (i) Is a vendor portal that forbids disclosure until a fix exists a step forward or a gag? (ii) Should researchers accept programs whose terms remove their timeline? (iii) Did publishing under threat help future researchers or only this case?

summary: Roth built a password-cracking tool running on Amazon EC2. His apartment was raided, his bank account frozen, and he was kept from releasing the tool at Black Hat DC; the injunction was later revoked and he published the research.
dilemmas: (i) Releasing a cheap, cloud-based cracking tool: defensive awareness or attacker uplift? (ii) Are raids and frozen accounts proportionate responses to a planned talk? (iii) Should dual-use tools be released openly or to vetted users only?

institution: Hari Prasad / ECIL Electronic Voting Machines (India)
summary: Prasad co-authored a 2010 paper showing vulnerabilities in India's electronic voting machines. Mumbai police arrested him and pressed him to reveal the anonymous source who provided the machine; he spent seven days in custody before release on bail. disclose.io also lists the case among incidents that crossed the line because the machine was allegedly stolen.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is research on an improperly obtained voting machine justified by the public interest in election integrity? (ii) Should researchers protect an anonymous source at personal legal risk? (iii) Does government pressure on election-security research undermine or protect public trust?

institution: Varun Uppal & Gyan Chawdhary / Financial Industry Client
summary: A talk on hacking high-speed trading systems was pulled from a security conference under financial pressure, the potential loss of a client, and was never presented elsewhere.
dilemmas: (i) Should a firm's client relationships decide whether research is published? (ii) Do markets benefit more from silence or from disclosure of trading-system flaws? (iii) Who represents the public interest when the only objector is a paying customer?

summary: Huang's Black Hat 2010 talk, an archaeological study of China's government-backed hacking from 2001 to 2010, was cancelled two weeks before the conference due to pressure from the Taiwanese government.
dilemmas: (i) When geopolitical concerns conflict with research publication, whose interests should prevail? (ii) Should researchers comply with pressure from a government that isn't their direct regulator? (iii) Does suppressing threat-actor research help or harm defenders?

institution: Scott Jarkoff (TechMiso) / RSA (Navy Federal Credit Union)
summary: Jarkoff's site published a report on security issues with Navy Federal Credit Union's website. RSA challenged the publication, and RSA backed down after TechMiso and its host pushed back.
dilemmas: (i) Should a security vendor act to suppress reporting about a client's website? (ii) Is publishing first justified when a financial institution's members are exposed? (iii) What role should hosting providers play when pressured to remove research?

summary: James published XSS and phishing vulnerabilities on Comerica Bank's website. Comerica sent a cease-and-desist to Tumblr, which removed the information while the vulnerability remained present.
dilemmas: (i) Removing the report while the flaw stays live: who does that protect? (ii) Should platforms honor takedowns of security research about unpatched flaws? (iii) Was public-first disclosure appropriate for a phishing-enabling bank flaw?

summary: HackersBlog published multiple vulnerabilities and intrusions affecting Orange.fr and later reported apparent legal threats, without publishing their details.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is publishing evidence of intrusions into a telecom's systems research or a breach? (ii) Do unpublished legal threats deserve the same weight as documented ones? (iii) How should groups that access data to prove flaws be judged?

summary: Sequoia threatened legal action over a planned independent examination of its voting machines, and a judge suppressed the resulting report on voting machine security; as of October 2008 it remained unpublished.
dilemmas: (i) Should voting machine vendors be able to block independent examination of systems used in public elections? (ii) Trade-secret claims versus voters' right to know. (iii) Should researchers accept engagements that a vendor can veto?

summary: Secunia published vulnerabilities in Autonomy's KeyView after Autonomy threatened legal action. Autonomy reportedly threatened CORE Security as well, which was not made public.
dilemmas: (i) Should researchers publicize threats they receive, or handle them quietly? (ii) Is it fair to the field when one firm resists a threat and another stays silent? (iii) Can legal threats against a widely embedded library ever serve its downstream users?

summary: Halvar Flake was denied entry into the United States on his way to teach security training, and the training was cancelled at the last minute.
dilemmas: (i) Should border authorities be able to block researchers from sharing defensive knowledge? (ii) How should international researchers weigh travel risk when presenting in other countries? (iii) Do conferences owe foreign speakers legal and logistical support?

summary: Karunaratne published information about a backdoor in routers supplied by his ISP, Be Unlimited. The ISP terminated his service; passwords were redacted, a patch was supplied, and his service had not been restored as of July 2007.
dilemmas: (i) Is publishing details of an ISP router backdoor justified when every customer is exposed? (ii) Is cutting off a customer's service a legitimate response or retaliation? (iii) Should passwords have been redacted before publication, not after?

summary: Paget's Black Hat DC talk on RFID security problems in HID access cards was pulled after a legal threat from HID, and the research was not published.
dilemmas: (i) Should a vendor be able to stop research on access-control cards protecting buildings? (ii) Does withholding RFID cloning research protect card holders or leave them unaware? (iii) Should an employer pull a talk to avoid litigation costs?

institution: David Maynor & Robert Graham (Errata Security) / TippingPoint
summary: Errata Security reverse-engineered TippingPoint's intrusion-prevention rule set to identify the vulnerabilities the rules protected against, drawing a threat from TippingPoint. The bulk of the research was later published at Black Hat 2007.
dilemmas: (i) Deriving unpatched vulnerabilities from a vendor's protection signatures: defensive research or zero-day harvesting? (ii) Does publishing the method endanger customers relying on those rules? (iii) Can IPS vendors keep signatures confidential without slowing defense?

summary: Researchers using the names Vipsta and MurderSkillz reported SQL injection flaws in 8pixel.net's SimpleBlog 2.3, an ASP-based blogging application.
