An incident archive reports that the vendor threatened legal action soon after notification; the researchers then published proof-of-concept material. The linked exploit alone does not establish the reported legal threat.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is releasing an exploit two days after a legal threat retaliation or protection of users? (ii) Should a threat end a researcher's duty to coordinate? (iii) How should small open-source theme authors handle reports they don't understand?

summary: Sybase threatened NGSSoftware over planned publication of database vulnerabilities. The threat was dropped and the research published.
dilemmas: (i) Should database customers learn about flaws even when the vendor objects to timing? (ii) Do license terms limit what researchers can say about benchmarked or tested software? (iii) Does a dropped threat still chill other researchers?

institution: Billy Hoffman & Virgil Griffith / Blackboard Transaction System
summary: Blackboard sent a cease-and-desist to the Interz0ne conference and filed a complaint against two students who planned to present flaws in its campus card transaction system. The parties reached a confidential agreement.
dilemmas: (i) Should vendors be able to stop students presenting flaws in campus systems they use daily? (ii) Do confidential settlements protect students or bury research? (iii) Does a vendor's repeated conflict with student researchers (see also Demirkapi) suggest a pattern worth weighing?

summary: Auriemma published vulnerabilities in the Unreal game engine and received a legal threat from Epic Games. The same day, Epic's Mark Rein apologized publicly, calling it a 'moment-of-stupidity' reaction.
dilemmas: (i) Does a quick public apology repair the chilling effect of a threat? (ii) Should game engines used by millions be held to enterprise disclosure norms? (iii) Should researchers coordinate with game vendors before publishing?

summary: HP invoked the DMCA in threatening SNOsoft over a Tru64 Unix vulnerability. The two later agreed on a disclosure timeline, and additional Tru64 vulnerabilities were published.
dilemmas: (i) Should copyright law apply to publishing an operating system vulnerability? (ii) Is a negotiated timeline after a threat a fair outcome? (iii) Did using the DMCA here set a precedent that helped or hurt the field?

summary: Tena published research showing weaknesses in Tegam's Viguard antivirus, contradicting its marketing claims. Tegam pursued him in French courts, which imposed a suspended fine of 5,000 euros.
dilemmas: (i) Should reverse engineering to test a security product's claims be treated as copyright infringement? (ii) Do consumers' interests in accurate antivirus marketing outweigh vendor IP? (iii) How should researchers in stricter jurisdictions publish product evaluations?

summary: A researcher reported authentication vulnerabilities in Wowza's media server; the vendor threatened to 'reevaluate' his independent consultant status, among other indirect threats. He disclosed after the vendor refused a remediation plan and left its consultant program. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
dilemmas: (i) When a researcher also earns income from the vendor, can disclosure decisions stay independent? (ii) Is threatening someone's business relationship a legal threat by another name? (iii) Should a vendor's refusal to share a remediation plan trigger disclosure?

summary: Miller found vulnerabilities in the Android-based T-Mobile G1, which Google downplayed. Years later he said Google went to his employer, later clarifying it was not a legal threat but a lecture on responsible disclosure to his boss. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
dilemmas: (i) Is contacting a researcher's employer a legitimate complaint or indirect pressure? (ii) Did speaking to the press before a patch serve G1 users? (iii) Where is the line between lecturing and threatening?

summary: Edge reportedly rescinded a Black Hat talk on FileVault encryption weaknesses after Apple invoked an existing NDA. Black Hat's CFP team found no record of the talk being submitted, and Attrition suggested the incident was used for publicity. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Should an NDA with a vendor override disclosure of flaws affecting all users? (ii) How should the community treat suppression claims that may be publicity? (iii) Should researchers under NDA research that vendor's products at all?

summary: Argeniss planned to publish one Oracle database vulnerability a day for a week to pressure Oracle over slow patching, then cancelled amid rumors of financial or legal threats. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is a public 'bug a day' campaign legitimate pressure or reckless exposure of customers? (ii) Should frustration with a vendor's patch speed justify releasing unpatched flaws? (iii) Do rumored threats chill research as much as real ones?

summary: A student used keyloggers on university computers to collect other students' credentials in order to expose security weaknesses, and was charged with computer crimes. disclose.io lists this among incidents that crossed the line.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Can collecting real users' credentials ever be justified to prove a system is insecure? (ii) Does a good motive excuse harm to classmates who never consented? (iii) What should a student do when an institution ignores warnings?

summary: Grutzmacher reported SNMP flaws in H3C and Huawei networking gear to US-CERT on August 6, 2012, and told the vendors they had until his ToorCon talk. Days before the conference, HP, H3C's parent company, asked him not to present because it was not ready; he agreed to cancel. HP published its advisory on October 22, and Grutzmacher published his findings the next day.
dilemmas: (i) Should researchers honor a polite vendor request to cancel when the vendor had months of notice? (ii) Was the request about protecting users or about the vendor's own timing? (iii) Does agreeing to cancel set an expectation that makes future requests harder to refuse?

institution: Sergey Gordeychik & Denis Baranov (Positive Technologies) / SCADA
summary: The researchers' DEF CON 20 talk, 'SCADA Strangelove: How I Learned To Start Worrying And Love The Nuclear Plants,' promised about 20 new vulnerabilities in SCADA systems including Siemens SIMATIC WinCC. They pulled it about a week before the conference and it was replaced with another talk; no reason was given, and reporters speculated about vendor pressure. They later presented SCADA Strangelove research at 29C3 in December 2012.
dilemmas: (i) How much industrial-control vulnerability detail, and what tools, are safe to release at a hacker conference? (ii) How should the community interpret a cancellation with no stated reason? (iii) Should ICS findings go through national CERTs and vendors before any public talk?

institution: Riley Hassell & Shane Macaulay / Google Android
summary: The Privateer Labs researchers did not appear for their scheduled Black Hat 2011 talk, 'Hacking Androids for Profit.' Hassell later said they withdrew to prevent an unacceptable window of risk to consumers and to make sure prior research was credited, and that they had alerted Google. Google said the identified bugs were not present in Android.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is withdrawing a talk over misuse fears responsible, or does it leave users uninformed? (ii) How should researchers handle discovering their work overlaps prior research? (iii) What should a vendor's public denial mean for the research's credibility?

institution: Dillon Beresford & Brian Meixell (NSS Labs) / Siemens & DHS
summary: Beresford and Brian Meixell pulled their TakeDownCon 2011 talk on Siemens PLC vulnerabilities after Siemens and DHS's ICS-CERT raised concerns; Siemens had found at the last minute that its planned mitigation did not work. Both researchers and NSS Labs said they were asked, not forced. Beresford presented the research at Black Hat in August 2011.
dilemmas: (i) Should government concern about critical infrastructure override a researcher's publication plan? (ii) Is voluntary withdrawal after an official request different from censorship? (iii) When a vendor's fix fails at the last minute, who should decide whether the talk goes ahead?

summary: Initial reports said ATM vendors threatened Chiesa into cancelling a Hack in the Box Europe talk. Chiesa said no threats were made and the cancellation was logistical; some in the industry called it a publicity stunt.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) How should media and the community verify suppression claims before amplifying them? (ii) Does publicity-driven framing harm researchers who face real threats? (iii) Should ATM research be presented publicly at all before banks patch?

summary: Juniper Networks pulled Barnaby Jack's Black Hat 2009 talk, 'Jackpotting Automated Teller Machines,' after the affected ATM vendor said its customers were not yet protected; Jack had reportedly worked with the vendor for months. After moving to IOActive, he demonstrated ATM jackpotting attacks at Black Hat 2010; Triton said it had patched in November 2009.
dilemmas: (i) Is a one-year delay a reasonable trade for giving operators time to patch ATMs? (ii) Should an employer, rather than the researcher, decide when a talk is ready? (iii) Does a live jackpotting demo inform defenders or instruct criminals?

institution: Aran Khanna / Harvard University / Facebook Messenger
summary: Harvard student Aran Khanna developed Marauder's Map, a browser extension that plotted location coordinates attached to Facebook Messenger messages and showed how they could reveal people's movements. After the extension attracted attention, Facebook asked him to remove it and withdrew an internship offer. Facebook subsequently changed Messenger's location-sharing behavior.
dilemmas: (i) Is it ethical to expose people's location just to demonstrate a privacy issue? (ii) Was publicly releasing the extension necessary? (iii) Is Facebook justified in withdrawing his internship? (iv) Is collecting existing data ethically different from creating new surveillance capabilities?

summary: Crypto AG, a Swiss encryption company, secretly operated under the ownership of the CIA and West German intelligence agency (BND), selling compromised encryption equipment to governments worldwide. Under Operation Rubicon, the agencies intercepted communications that customers believed were secure, including those of governments implicated in human rights abuses. A 2020 investigation by The Washington Post, ZDF, and SRF exposed the operation and raised ethical questions about government deception, the exploitation of commercial trust, and intelligence agencies' responsibility to act on information about human rights violations.
dilemmas: (i) Is deceiving customers acceptable for national security? (ii) Should intelligence agencies act on what they learn about human rights abuses, or protect the source? (iii) Does a case like this damage trust in all encryption vendors?

summary: Under Operation Trojan Shield, the FBI and international partners secretly operated the ANOM encrypted-phone platform and distributed it through criminal networks. Messages were copied to investigators, leading to coordinated arrests announced in 2021. The operation raised questions about covert monitoring and cross-border legal safeguards.
dilemmas: (i) Is it acceptable for police to run a deceptive “secure” product? (ii) Should agencies be able to route around domestic legal limits through foreign partners? (iii) Does this make people less willing to trust real privacy tools?

summary: Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, was malware designed to disrupt industrial control equipment associated with uranium enrichment at Iran's Natanz facility. It is widely attributed to the United States and Israel, although neither has publicly acknowledged responsibility. Its spread beyond the intended environment illustrated how offensive cyber operations can create risks outside their targets.
dilemmas: (i) Is a cyberattack on infrastructure different from a conventional strike? (ii) Is it acceptable to hoard and use zero-days that leave everyone else vulnerable? (iii) Who is accountable when the code escapes its target?

summary: Between 2016 and 2017, the Shadow Brokers released tools linked to the U.S. National Security Agency, including the Windows exploit known as EternalBlue. Microsoft patched the underlying vulnerability in March 2017, but the exploit's subsequent public release contributed to attacks such as WannaCry and NotPetya on systems that remained unpatched.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: No charges filed for the leak itself
dilemmas: (i) Should governments keep zero-days for intelligence or disclose them to vendors? (ii) Who is responsible for the harm the leaked exploit caused? (iii) How should exploit retention be overseen?

institution: Apple v. FBI / San Bernardino iPhone
summary: Following the 2015 San Bernardino terrorist attack, the FBI sought an order requiring Apple to help unlock an attacker's iPhone without triggering its passcode protections. Apple opposed the order, arguing that creating the requested software would weaken user security more broadly. The government withdrew the request in March 2016 after gaining access through an outside party.
outcome: FBI withdrew court order after third-party access
dilemmas: (i) Can a company be forced to weaken its own security? (ii) One phone vs. every user’s security: what responsibility does the outside party that unlocked it have?

summary: In July 2021, the REvil group exploited vulnerabilities in Kaseya's VSA management software, spreading ransomware through managed service providers to downstream organizations. Dutch researchers had reported related flaws to Kaseya before the attack. The incident highlighted the difficulty of coordinating vulnerability disclosure and patch deployment across complex software supply chains.
outcome: Ransomware incident; recovery and law-enforcement actions
dilemmas: (i) How quickly should vendors act when researchers report vulnerabilities in software used by many downstream organizations?; (ii) What responsibilities do managed service providers have to their customers during supply-chain incidents?; (iii) Should a patch timeline be accelerated when exploitation appears imminent?; (iv) How should vendors and researchers coordinate warnings without aiding attackers?

summary: In early 2021, attackers exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft Exchange servers and installed web shells for persistent access. Microsoft issued security updates, but patching alone did not remove already-installed shells. In April, the U.S. Justice Department announced a court-authorized FBI operation to remove malicious web shells from hundreds of U.S. servers without advance owner consent.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Should the government be able to access private systems without consent to fix a security problem? (ii) Who is responsible for cleanup when owners cannot or will not do it? (iii) Does a court order make it ethical if owners are not told first?

summary: On July 19, 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike Falcon content update caused widespread crashes on Windows systems, disrupting airlines, hospitals, and other services. The incident was not a cyberattack. Restoring many affected machines required manual intervention, and CrowdStrike subsequently published technical explanations and changes to its testing and rollout process.
dilemmas: (i) Should security vendors be liable for outages their products cause? (ii) Does deep system access by security tools create too much risk for the protection it gives? (iii) How fast should urgent security updates ship vs. how carefully should they be tested?

summary: In 2020, French and Dutch authorities compromised the EncroChat encrypted-phone network used by many organized-crime groups and obtained large volumes of messages for criminal investigations. The operation led to thousands of arrests, while defendants in several countries challenged the legality and admissibility of the collected evidence.
dilemmas: (i) Is it acceptable to hack every user of a service if most are suspected criminals? (ii) Should defendants be able to challenge evidence when the technique stays secret? (iii) What happens to legitimate users caught up in the operation?

summary: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160), disclosed in April 2014, was a flaw in OpenSSL's heartbeat extension that could expose portions of server or client memory, including potentially sensitive credentials and cryptographic material. Coordinated patching and public warnings raised questions about the timing of disclosure for widely deployed open-source infrastructure.
dilemmas: (i) What obligations do maintainers of widely deployed security libraries have when their project is underfunded? (ii) How should organizations and funders distribute responsibility for software that is free to use but critical to security?

summary: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), disclosed in December 2021, was a critical remote-code-execution flaw in the widely used Apache Log4j logging library. Maintainers issued urgent fixes while organizations struggled to locate affected dependencies and attackers rapidly exploited vulnerable systems. The incident highlighted the burden placed on volunteer-led open-source projects.
dilemmas: (i) Who should bear responsibility for flaws in widely used volunteer-run software? (ii) Should disclosure be delayed, or sped up, once exploitation starts? (iii) What do companies owe the open source projects they depend on?

institution: Joshua Schulte / Vault 7 / CIA cyber-tool disclosures
summary: In 2017, WikiLeaks began publishing documents about CIA cyber tools under the name Vault 7, revealing techniques used against computers, phones, and connected devices. The disclosures stimulated public debate but also raised concerns about exposing offensive capabilities. Former CIA engineer Joshua Schulte was later convicted of crimes connected to the theft and disclosure of the files.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Criminal prosecution of source; public disclosures
dilemmas: (i) Is publishing details of government hacking tools in the public interest or a security risk? (ii) How much should a publisher redact? (iii) Is the leaker a whistleblower or a criminal?

summary: In 2013, former intelligence contractor Edward Snowden gave journalists classified documents revealing U.S. surveillance programs, including bulk collection of telephone metadata. The disclosures prompted major public debate and policy changes, while the U.S. government charged Snowden under the Espionage Act. The case raises questions about secrecy, public-interest reporting, and whistleblower protections.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Charges filed; Snowden remains in exile
dilemmas: (i) Is breaking secrecy obligations justified when the programs may be unlawful? (ii) Should he have used internal channels first? (iii) How should whistleblowers be protected, given there is no real public-interest defense under the Espionage Act?

summary: In 2015, a group calling itself the Impact Team stole and published personal information from the Ashley Madison dating service after demanding that it close. The disclosure exposed millions of users to privacy harms, extortion attempts, and public scrutiny. Privacy regulators later criticized the operator's information-security and privacy practices, while the attackers' claimed moral purpose raised questions about harming users to punish a company.
outcome: Data published; litigation and extortion concerns
dilemmas: (i) Is it acceptable to punish a company for its practices by exposing its users? (ii) Is it ethical for researchers and journalists to analyze or report on stolen personal data? (iii) Do people who used the service deserve less privacy protection?

institution: Xiaofeng Wang / Indiana University Federal Investigation
summary: In March 2025, federal agents searched homes associated with Indiana University cybersecurity professor Xiaofeng Wang and his wife, Nianli Ma, while the university terminated their employment. Reporting described a separate institutional inquiry into possible research-funding disclosures, but public evidence did not establish wrongdoing. Their lawyers said they had not been arrested or charged. The events raised questions about academic due process, research collaboration, and the presumption of innocence.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Federal investigation reported; no criminal charges publicly announced at the time of reporting
dilemmas: (i) How should universities safeguard due process while responding to federal investigations?; (ii) When does scrutiny of international research funding risk stigmatizing legitimate collaboration?; (iii) What information should institutions disclose when allegations remain unproven?; (iv) How can research-integrity procedures avoid causing disproportionate reputational harm?

institution: Dennis Giese and Braelynn Luedtke / Ecovacs Robot Security
summary: Security researchers Dennis Giese and Braelynn Luedtke reported vulnerabilities in Ecovacs robot vacuums that could allow unauthorized access to connected devices and their sensors. Their work raised questions about the security and privacy of smart-home devices and the appropriate timing of public disclosure.
outcome: Public research disclosure and subsequent vendor security advisories
dilemmas: (i) Should device owners be able to inspect and modify firmware despite vendor restrictions?; (ii) How much exploit detail is appropriate when it can help both defenders and attackers?; (iii) What privacy obligations arise when household sensors send data to vendor cloud services?; (iv) How can researchers promote user control without introducing new risks?

summary: Security researchers from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz discovered critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and coordinated disclosure with the PHP security team and distributors. The public release was scheduled for October 22, 2026. On October 20, an anonymous user prematurely leaked information about the vulnerabilities online, which spread through social media. Although the initial leak did not contain technical exploit details, a subsequent premature video release by Calif and an early patch distribution by Chainguard further disrupted the embargo. The PHP security team accelerated its release schedule to October 21, 2026, to reduce exposure before coordinated patches became available.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is it ethical to disclose critical vulnerabilities before patches are available, even when disclosure could pressure vendors to respond faster? (ii) Do individuals who obtain confidential vulnerability information have an ethical obligation to respect coordinated disclosure agreements? (iii) Should researchers prioritize public awareness or adherence to disclosure timelines when millions of systems may be vulnerable? (iv) What responsibilities do researchers and distributors have when premature disclosures expose users to exploitation before patches are widely available?
